# Estimation {.unnumbered} *Session 1 ended one number short. This chapter carries the vocabulary you need to supply that number in the room, and stops before supplying it. Read it, do the self-test, and bring your five bean masses.* ## Where we stopped The workshop established three things, and you generated all three rather than being told them: 1. The sample means were centred in the same place as the individual beans. 2. The means were narrower than the beans, and narrower again at $n = 20$. 3. Nobody's mean was the population mean. The second fact is the useful one and it is the one left incomplete. You know the sampling distribution is narrower. You do not know by how much, and until you do you cannot say how far your own number might be from the truth. From here on the beans are a teaching device and the problem is a real one. ## Darwin's maize {#sec-darwin} In 1876 Charles Darwin published the results of an experiment on inbreeding [@darwin1876]. He raised maize plants (*Zea mays*) in matched pairs: in each pot, one plant grown from a cross-fertilised seed and one from a self-fertilised seed, sown at the same time and kept under the same conditions. Fifteen pairs, thirty plants. He measured final height in inches. The dataset you will use for the rest of Block 1 is exactly those thirty numbers. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} group_means <- darwin |> summarise(mean_height = mean(height), .by = type) ggplot(darwin, aes(x = type, y = height)) + geom_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, colour = house_col, size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) + geom_errorbar( data = group_means, aes(y = mean_height, ymin = mean_height, ymax = mean_height), width = 0.35, linewidth = 0.6 ) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Final height (inches)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Darwin's thirty maize plants. Each point is one plant; the horizontal bars mark the two group means. Cross-fertilised plants averaged about 2.6 inches taller, but the two groups overlap heavily and two cross-fertilised plants were shorter than all but one selfed plant.](02-estimation_files/figure-html/fig-darwin-1.png){#fig-darwin width=672} ::: ::: Darwin's difficulty was not measuring the plants. It was deciding whether the gap between those two bars meant anything. Cross-fertilised plants were taller on average, but individual plants varied so much that the tallest selfed plant beat most of the cross-fertilised ones. He was aware of the problem and could not solve it; he sent the numbers to his cousin Francis Galton, and the question of what to do with them remained open for another fifty years. That is the problem this session begins on. ::: {.callout-note} ## Two things we are deliberately not doing yet **We are not comparing the groups.** Deciding whether a difference between two means is real is Session 3, and the linear model that formalises it is Session 4. Before any of that, you have to be able to describe *one* mean and say how uncertain it is, so this session works with the fifteen **cross-fertilised** plants alone. **We are not using the pairing.** Darwin's design pairs each plant with a partner in the same pot, and that pairing is the most informative feature of the data. Session 3 uses it. ::: ## Signal and noise {#sec-signal} Every biological measurement is two things added together: a systematic part shared by every individual in the population, and a departure from it that is different for every individual. $$\text{measurement} = \text{signal} + \text{noise}$$ For the maize, the signal is the typical height of a cross-fertilised plant grown under Darwin's conditions. The noise is the amount by which any particular plant departs from typical, because of its genotype, its position in the pot, the seed it happened to grow from. The signal is what you are trying to learn. The noise is why learning it is difficult. Look again at @fig-darwin with that expression in mind. The signal Darwin was chasing, the difference between the two treatments, is about 2.6 inches. The noise, the typical distance between one plant and its own group's mean, is larger than that. **The signal is smaller than the noise.** That is the ordinary situation in biology, and it is the reason statistics exists as a discipline rather than as an afterthought. Two consequences follow, and they organise the rest of Block 1. **A dataset answers two separate questions and you need both.** *Where is the centre?* is answered by the mean. *How far do individuals sit from it?* is answered by a measure of spread. Neither implies the other, and a mean reported on its own is an incomplete description. **The noise is why your sample mean was wrong.** Your five beans carried five departures from typical. They did not cancel exactly, and what was left over is the distance between your mean and the truth. Darwin's fifteen plants carried fifteen departures, and the same is true of his. ::: {.callout-warning} ## "Noise" does not mean "error" The word is borrowed from engineering and it misleads in biology. Variation between individuals is not a defect in your data. It is a property of the population, and frequently the property you care about most: it is what selection acts on and what a great deal of biology is the study of. It is also not one thing. Two sources are mixed together in any real dataset: - **biological variation**, which is real and belongs to the population; - **measurement error**, which is introduced by you, your instrument and your observers, and belongs to your method. The statistics in this module cannot separate them. Both widen the data in exactly the same way and every technique here treats them identically. Only your design can tell them apart, by measuring the same individual twice. ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## What "population" means from here on Darwin measured fifteen cross-fertilised plants. He was not interested in those fifteen. He was interested in what cross-fertilisation does to maize, which is a claim about plants he never grew. So the population here is not a list of individuals. It is a **process**: whatever combination of genetics, soil and season produces cross-fertilised maize plants of some typical height with some typical variation. The signal-plus-noise expression above is a description of exactly such a process, and the fifteen plants are fifteen values it happened to produce. This is a change from Session 1, where the population was a finite tub of beans that could in principle have been weighed entirely. The arithmetic barely notices. The reasoning does, because a process can produce values you have never seen, and the linear model in Session 4 is a statement about a process. ::: ## Measuring the noise: the standard deviation {#sec-sd} The **standard deviation** measures the noise. Loosely, it is the typical distance between an individual and the mean, in the units of the measurement. For Darwin's cross-fertilised plants it is about 3.6 inches, so plants sit roughly three and a half inches away from typical, some more, some less. ### What a standard deviation buys you On its own that is just a number attached to a dataset. Combined with an assumption it becomes a statement about where individual plants sit. The assumption is that the process generating the plants is approximately normal. If it is, Session 1's 68-95-99.7 rule applies, and the abstract axis in that figure can be relabelled in inches. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} mu <- mean(cross$height) sigma <- sd(cross$height) normal_curve <- tibble(height = seq(mu - 4 * sigma, mu + 4 * sigma, length.out = 1000)) |> mutate(density = dnorm(height, mu, sigma)) band_region <- function(lo, hi, band, piece) { tibble(height = seq(mu + lo * sigma, mu + hi * sigma, length.out = 400)) |> mutate(density = dnorm(height, mu, sigma), band = band, piece = piece) } bands <- bind_rows( band_region(-1, 1, "Within 1 SD", 1), band_region(-2, -1, "1 to 2 SD", 2), band_region(1, 2, "1 to 2 SD", 3), band_region(-3, -2, "2 to 3 SD", 4), band_region(2, 3, "2 to 3 SD", 5) ) |> mutate(band = factor(band, levels = c("Within 1 SD", "1 to 2 SD", "2 to 3 SD"))) sd_axis <- scale_x_continuous( breaks = mu + (-3:3) * sigma, labels = \(x) round(x, 1) ) ggplot(mapping = aes(height, density)) + geom_area(data = bands, aes(alpha = band, group = piece), fill = house_col) + geom_line(data = normal_curve, linewidth = 0.8) + scale_alpha_manual(values = c(0.65, 0.40, 0.20)) + sd_axis + labs(x = "Final height (inches)", y = "Probability density", alpha = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A normal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation as Darwin's cross-fertilised plants. The axis is in inches rather than in standard deviations, and the ticks are placed one standard deviation apart. The shaded bands hold about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of the area cumulatively.](02-estimation_files/figure-html/fig-normal-maize-1.png){#fig-normal-maize width=672} ::: ::: Read off the axis and the rule says something concrete. If cross-fertilised maize really is normally distributed with this mean and this standard deviation, then about 68% of plants stand between 16.6 and 23.8 inches, about 95% between 13.0 and 27.4, and virtually all between 9.3 and 31.0. That is a claim about the process, and Darwin's fifteen plants are the only evidence we have on whether it holds. @fig-normal-plants puts them on the same axis. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} bin_width <- 0.5 # plants within half an inch of each other get stacked dot_gap <- 0.008 # vertical spacing between stacked points plants <- cross |> arrange(height) |> mutate(bin = floor(height / bin_width)) |> mutate(stack = row_number(), .by = bin) |> mutate(y = -dot_gap * stack) ggplot(mapping = aes(height, density)) + geom_area(data = bands, aes(alpha = band, group = piece), fill = house_col) + geom_line(data = normal_curve, linewidth = 0.8) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) + geom_point( data = plants, aes(x = height, y = y), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.2, shape = 21, colour = "black" ) + scale_alpha_manual(values = c(0.65, 0.40, 0.20)) + sd_axis + labs(x = "Final height (inches)", y = "Probability density", alpha = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The same curve with Darwin's fifteen cross-fertilised plants beneath it, one point per plant. Points are stacked where two plants had the same recorded height. The two shortest plants, both 12 inches, sit outside the two standard deviation band.](02-estimation_files/figure-html/fig-normal-plants-1.png){#fig-normal-plants width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.webex-check .webex-box} Count the points in @fig-normal-plants before answering. There are fifteen. How many plants fall within one standard deviation of the mean, that is between 16.6 and 23.8 inches? How many fall within two standard deviations, between 13.0 and 27.4 inches? Expressed as percentages those counts are 87% and 87%, against the 68% and 95% the rule predicts. The reasonable conclusion is that
::: The mismatch is worth sitting with for a moment. Thirteen of fifteen inside one standard deviation is more than the rule leads you to expect, and two plants outside two standard deviations is more than the 0.75 plants you would expect. Neither departure is large enough to conclude anything: with fifteen observations the counts move by whole plants, so 87% and 68% are not far apart in any meaningful sense. That cuts both ways, and it is the honest position. **You cannot tell from fifteen points whether a population is normal**, and you should be suspicious of anyone who claims to. Session 8 gives you the tools for asking the question properly. ::: {.callout-note} ## Two standard deviations, or 1.96? Session 1 gave the rule as 95% within two standard deviations, which is the version worth memorising. The exact multiplier for 95% is 1.96, and two is a rounding of it. The difference is invisible in a figure and matters when you compute an interval by hand, which you will do in the workshop. Use 1.96 when you are calculating and two when you are thinking. ::: It has one property worth stating explicitly, because it is the hinge of the next section. **The standard deviation does not shrink as you collect more data.** Had Darwin grown fifteen hundred cross-fertilised plants instead of fifteen, the standard deviation would have settled near the same value. This is not a limitation. Maize plants genuinely are that variable, and a larger sample measures the variability more precisely rather than reducing it. ::: {.callout-note} ## Why R divides by $n - 1$ A small sample rarely happens to include the extremes, so the spread you observe is systematically narrower than the spread of the process. Dividing the squared deviations by $n - 1$ rather than $n$ inflates the answer by just enough to correct that on average. `sd()` and `var()` already do this, so it asks nothing of you. It is worth knowing because it makes explicit that the number R returns is an estimate of the population's noise, not merely a description of your fifteen plants. The computing hour demonstrates the bias as a stretch task. ::: ## Noise in the estimate: the standard error {#sec-se} Now apply the same idea one level up. Darwin's mean of 20.2 inches is not the population mean. It sits some distance away, and that distance is the leftover noise carried through the arithmetic. Had he grown a fresh fifteen plants the following season he would have got a different mean and a different distance. Those repeats form the sampling distribution, and the sampling distribution has a spread of its own, which can be measured with a standard deviation exactly like any other spread. That number has its own name. The standard deviation of a sampling distribution is called the **standard error**. We cannot show you Darwin's repeats, because he only ran the experiment once, which is the ordinary situation. What we can do is take the process implied by his data and run it twenty times. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} sim <- withr::with_seed(demo_seed, { tibble(repeat_id = 1:20) |> mutate(height = map(repeat_id, \(i) rnorm(15, mean(cross$height), sd(cross$height)))) |> unnest(height) }) sim_means <- sim |> summarise(mean_height = mean(height), .by = repeat_id) ggplot(sim, aes(x = repeat_id, y = height)) + geom_point(colour = house_col, alpha = 0.35, size = 1.8) + geom_point(data = sim_means, aes(y = mean_height), size = 2.4) + geom_hline(yintercept = mean(cross$height), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) + labs(x = "Simulated repeat of the experiment", y = "Final height (inches)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Twenty simulated repeats of Darwin's experiment, each growing fifteen cross-fertilised plants from a process with the same signal and noise as his. Pale points are individual plants, dark points are the mean of each repeat, and the dashed line is the process mean. The plants scatter widely; the means scatter much less, and they are still not identical to one another.](02-estimation_files/figure-html/fig-repeats-1.png){#fig-repeats width=672} ::: ::: So there are two spreads in play, both in inches, both readable off the same axis: - the spread of the **individual plants**, which is a standard deviation, and answers *how variable are maize plants?* - the spread of the **experiment means**, which is a standard error, and answers *how variable is my answer?* The first belongs to the population and is fixed. The second belongs to your procedure, and shrinks when you grow more plants, exactly as the bean board showed when benches pooled to twenty. ::: {.callout-warning} ## SD and SE are not two names for one number They are computed from different things and answer different questions, but they are indistinguishable on the page. Both are positive, both are in inches, both appear after a $\pm$, and nothing in the output announces which you are looking at. Reporting one when you meant the other is among the most common numerical errors in the biological literature. Whenever you meet either, ask one question: **the spread of what?** If the answer is "the measurements", it is a standard deviation. If the answer is "the estimate", it is a standard error. ::: What you do not yet have is the rate. Doubling the sample does not halve the standard error, and the board told you as much: the means of twenty were tighter than the means of five, but visibly not four times tighter. There is a short expression relating the two spreads, and it involves the standard deviation and the sample size. **Do not look it up.** You will recover it from the board in the first hour, and recovering it is worth more than reading it. ## The central limit theorem {#sec-clt} The stretch task at the end of the computing hour asked you to replace the beans with a deliberately horrible population, most values near zero with a long right tail, and to look at the shape of the means. They came out close to a bell. That result has a name. The **central limit theorem** states that as sample size increases, the sampling distribution of the mean 1. stays centred on the population mean, 2. narrows, at a rate the theorem specifies exactly, and 3. approaches a normal distribution, **whatever the shape of the population**. Claims 1 and 2 you observed on the board. Claim 3 is the surprising one, and it is why the normal distribution runs through the rest of this module. Not because biological measurements are normal, which they frequently are not, but because the *estimates* computed from them behave normally almost regardless. Sessions 3 and 4 both reason about a statistic by treating its sampling distribution as normal, and this theorem is the licence for doing so. The theorem is not unconditional. It requires observations independent of one another, a population with finite variance, and a sample size that is not tiny. How large is large enough depends on how skewed the population is: for something mildly asymmetric ten will do, and for the exponential population in the stretch task thirty was plainly sufficient. Darwin's fifteen are not obviously comfortable on that scale, and @fig-darwin shows why: two of his cross-fertilised plants reached only 12 inches, well below the rest. Whether fifteen observations with a tail like that behave well enough is a real question, and it is asked properly in Session 8. ::: {.callout-warning} ## What the theorem does not do The central limit theorem describes the sampling distribution of a **random** sample. If the sampling scheme is biased, as with the "grabbed" beans in Session 1, the sampling distribution is still tidy and still approximately normal. It is simply centred on the wrong value, and a larger sample tightens it around that wrong value. Nothing in this session repairs a bad sample. Everything here quantifies noise, and bias is not noise. ::: ## Reporting both: the confidence interval {#sec-ci} "Cross-fertilised maize reaches 20.2 inches" has an awkward property as a conclusion: it is essentially certain to be wrong. Nobody in the room got the bean tub exactly right, Darwin did not get maize exactly right, and with a continuous measurement nobody ever will. The alternative is to report a range wide enough to reflect the noise remaining in the estimate. A **confidence interval** is a range calculated from your sample by a stated rule, where the rule is designed to succeed a specified proportion of the time. A 95% interval is a rule that succeeds 95% of the time. Notice that this sentence describes the *rule*, not the particular interval you happen to be holding. The difference between those two readings is the hardest idea in the session and the one you should not expect to absorb from a page. You will build forty intervals in the room, from the room's own beans, and count how many of them succeed. Before then, commit to an answer, in the same spirit as last week's guess at the tub. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: write one sentence and bring it** :::: ::::{.task-container} Darwin's fifteen cross-fertilised plants give a mean height of 20.2 inches with a 95% confidence interval from 18.2 to 22.2 inches. Write down, in one sentence and in your own words, what you think that interval tells you. Do not look it up, do not ask an AI assistant, and do not confer. Bring the sentence to the workshop. It is not assessed and nobody will collect it. Most people, including a majority of the researchers and methods instructors who have been asked directly, write down the same wrong sentence, and discovering that you are in that majority is the fastest route to remembering the right one [@hoekstra2014]. :::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Why this module is frequentist Session 1 defined probability as a long-run frequency and flagged that a second definition exists. It is time to name it. The **Bayesian** reading treats a probability as a degree of belief, which permits probability statements about things that happen only once, including about the true mean height of cross-fertilised maize. The two schools produce interval estimates that look similar and answer different questions. Neither is a defective version of the other. The workshop spends ten minutes on the contrast at the point where it becomes concrete, which is the interval above. This module is frequentist because its destination is the linear model, and the overwhelming majority of the biological literature you will read reports frequentist quantities. Reading them correctly comes before choosing otherwise. ::: ## Before the workshop :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: bring your beans** :::: ::::{.task-container} The first hour uses the numbers this room generated last week. Bring: - your five individual bean masses from Session 1, - your sample mean, - your sentence about Darwin's interval. If you were not there, generate five bean masses using the catch-up code in the Session 1 workshop chapter and bring those instead. :::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: check your vocabulary** :::: ::::{.task-container} Nothing is recorded and nothing is marked. Its only job is to tell you, and me, whether the vocabulary has landed before the room needs it. ::: {.webex-check .webex-box} In the expression *measurement = signal + noise*, the quantity estimated by the sample mean is the . ::: :::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## This is the session that most often goes wrong Two hours is not long for a standard error, a theorem and an interval, and the material is cumulative: the interval is built from the standard error, which is built from the sampling distribution you constructed last week. If any part of Session 1 is still shaky, twenty minutes rereading it before the workshop are the best-spent twenty minutes of the module. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## A note on sources The maize data are Darwin's own, published in *The Effects of Cross and Self Fertilisation in the Vegetable Kingdom* [@darwin1876] and reproduced many times since. The treatment of estimation and of confidence intervals is adapted from Chapter 10 of Danielle Navarro's *Learning Statistics with R* [@navarro2019], used and redistributed here under its CC BY-SA 4.0 licence. The examples have been rewritten for biology, and any errors introduced in doing so are ours. The evidence that confidence intervals are widely misread is from @hoekstra2014; the stronger argument that this is not merely a teaching failure is made by @morey2016. :::
